When something is not immediately obvious — when it needs to be figured out, explained, or made sense of — the explanation or understanding you arrive at is called an interpretation.

Think of it this way: you see something, hear something, or read something, and you ask yourself "What does this mean?" The answer you come up with — that is your interpretation.

Imagine you receive a text from a friend that says: "Sure, I'll come." But their tone in person lately has been cold. You might wonder — do they genuinely want to come, or are they just being polite? You think about it and decide: "I think they're just saying yes to avoid conflict."

That conclusion you reached? That's an interpretation. It's your understanding of something that wasn't perfectly clear on its own.

Now here's the key point: interpretation always involves a gap. A gap between what is directly shown or said and what it actually means. Interpretation is the bridge you build across that gap.
The Three Big Dimensions of This Word

The word "interpretation" is used in three broad, related ways:

1. Making Sense of Something Unclear or Complex

This is the most common use. Whenever something — a text, an event, a situation, a law, a dream, a piece of data — is not self-explanatory, you need to interpret it. The interpretation is what you conclude it means.

  • A lawyer reads a contract clause and gives an interpretation of what it legally requires.
  • A doctor looks at an X-ray and offers an interpretation of what the image shows about a patient's health.
  • A student reads a Shakespeare play and writes an interpretation of what a certain speech is trying to say.
  • A person wakes up from a vivid dream and tries to come up with an interpretation of what it might mean.

In all these cases, the raw material (the clause, the X-ray, the speech, the dream) exists on its own. But its meaning is not stamped on its face. You have to think, reason, and judge — and what you conclude is the interpretation.

2. A Personal or Particular Understanding (Often One of Many)

Interpretation also refers to the fact that the same thing can be understood in more than one way. When we say "an interpretation," we are often hinting that this is one possible reading among others that might exist.

  • "That is just your interpretation." — meaning: you understood it that way, but someone else might understand it differently.
  • "There are many possible interpretations of this poem." — meaning: reasonable people can read it in different valid ways.

This use of the word carries an important truth: interpretation is often subjective. It is shaped by who you are, what you know, what you believe, and what experiences you bring with you. Two honest, intelligent people can look at the same thing and arrive at different — yet both reasonable — interpretations.

This is why we say that facts are facts, but interpretations are not facts. A fact is something that simply is. An interpretation is someone's reading of what that fact means.

For example:

  • Fact: Sales dropped by 20% this quarter.
  • Interpretation A: The product is failing and needs to be discontinued.
  • Interpretation B: The market is seasonal and will recover next quarter.

Both interpretations are based on the same fact, but they explain it differently.

3. A Performed or Artistic Version of Something

In music, theatre, dance, and the arts generally, "interpretation" refers to the unique, personal way a performer brings a piece to life.

When a pianist plays a Beethoven sonata, the notes on the page are fixed. But how they play it — the pace, the emotion, the emphasis, the feeling — is their interpretation. Two great pianists can play the exact same piece, and each performance feels different, because each is a different interpretation.

Similarly:

  • An actor's interpretation of a character is the specific way they choose to portray that character's personality, motivations, and emotions.
  • A director's interpretation of a script is the overall vision they bring to how the story is told on stage or screen.

Here, interpretation means: "This is my understanding of what this work is, and here is how I express that understanding."
What All Three Uses Have in Common

Whether we're talking about analyzing a contract, disagreeing with a friend about what something meant, or watching a pianist perform — the word "interpretation" always involves:

  1. Something that exists (a text, an event, a piece of music, a situation)
  2. A mind engaging with it — thinking, feeling, reasoning
  3. A meaning or understanding that results — the interpretation itself

The thing itself doesn't give you a ready-made answer. Interpretation is the human act of finding or creating meaning from something that requires thought.
The Important Difference: Interpretation vs. Fact

This is crucial to understand.

A fact is verifiable and the same for everyone: "The building is 300 meters tall."

An interpretation is a reasoned understanding that may vary: "The building was built that tall to intimidate people" — maybe, maybe not. That's a reading, a conclusion, an interpretation.

Confusing the two is one of the most common mistakes people make in arguments. Someone states their interpretation as if it is a fact. Knowing the word "interpretation" helps you recognize this clearly.
Shades of Meaning: What It Implies

When you call something an interpretation, you are implying several things quietly:

  • Judgment was involved. It didn't just read itself — someone had to make a call.
  • Other readings may exist. Your interpretation is not necessarily the only possible one.
  • It can be more or less well-supported. A good interpretation is backed by evidence and reasoning. A weak one is not.
  • It is not random. An interpretation is not a wild guess. It is a thoughtful, reasoned conclusion — even if others might disagree with it.

• In law: A judge offers an interpretation of a constitutional clause to decide whether a new law is valid.
  • In religion: Different communities hold different interpretations of the same scripture.
  • In science: Researchers debate the interpretation of experimental results — what do the numbers actually tell us?
  • In history: Historians offer competing interpretations of why a war started.
  • In everyday life: "I think his silence means he's angry." — That's an interpretation of behavior.
  • In art: Each reader of a novel brings their own interpretation to what the ending means.

Interpretation is the meaning, explanation, or understanding that a person arrives at when they engage with something that is not self-explanatory — and it is always, to some degree, shaped by the person doing the interpreting.
